# Membership Is the Job

Source: https://lowob.com/research/membership-is-the-job/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-07-17 · Updated: 2026-11-17
Function: Growth

> Summary: A media audience is a list until it becomes a membership: people who pay, show up, contribute and refer. With only 17% paying for online news across 20 markets in 2026, membership has to offer more than access. Build it on sourcing, peer amplification and peer value, keep it on channels you control, and measure it monthly like a business line.

A media audience is a list until it is a membership. Build the membership on sourcing, amplification and peer value, then measure it like a business line. The market makes the case: the Reuters Institute's 2026 Digital News Report found 17% of people across 20 paywall-heavy markets paid for online news, flat on the year, and reach of publishers' own sites and apps down 12 percentage points since 2021.

This is the media chapter of our [guide to building a community that lasts](https://lowob.com/research/building-a-community-that-lasts/).

## The number that is not a community

Media founders report audience numbers because they are easy to count. Subscribers, followers, opens, downloads. None of these are a community. A community is a set of people with a relationship to you and to each other.

Our piece [An audience is not a business](https://lowob.com/research/an-audience-is-not-a-business/) made the point that an audience does not pay the bills on its own. The same logic applies here. An audience is not a community either. It is the pool you recruit a community from.

[Community is a job, not a number](https://lowob.com/research/community-is-a-job-not-a-number/) defined community as a job with an owner, a budget and a measure. In media the job is membership. The output is people who pay, show up, contribute and refer. If a person does none of those four things, they are a reader, not a member.

The pool is harder to convert than it was. The Reuters Institute surveyed 97,520 people in 48 markets for its 2026 report. Across the 20 markets where paywalls are common, 17% paid for online news, with falls of four points in the US and six in Austria. Most payers (81%) cited direct benefits, but 46% also gave values-based reasons, such as supporting journalism. The Membership Puzzle Project, a research collaboration between NYU's Jay Rosen and De Correspondent that ran from 2017 to 2021, defined membership as "a social contract between a news organization and the community it serves", in which members give time, money and ideas. Its review of nearly 100 membership models concluded that "no one has ever become an enthusiastic member of a commodity news site."

## The three contributions that matter

Members do a lot of things. Three of them change the business.

**Sourcing.** Members send tips, data, documents and questions. The best stories in niche media come from the people closest to the subject. A member who sends one good lead a quarter is worth more than a thousand passive subscribers. Make it easy: a standing inbox, a members' thread, an editor who replies within a day. The Membership Puzzle Project documented members contributing tips, expertise, moderation and co-reporting across the sites it studied.

**Amplification, but the right kind.** You do not need members who post your work to the public. You need members who forward it to the three peers who matter. Niche media grows through private channels: a message to a colleague, a mention in a team meeting. Ask for that explicitly. "Who on your team should see this?" beats "please share."

**Peer value.** This is the one that holds. Members who want access to each other will stay through a bad month of content. A platform can copy your format and outbid you for writers. It cannot copy a room of people who already trust each other. Everything in the design below serves this.

Expect the contributions to come from a few. Participation research consistently finds a small core doing most of the work: in one study of four online networks, the top 1% of members wrote about 75% of posts. A contribution rate of a few percent is normal. The aim is to know who those people are and keep them.

> A platform can copy your format and outbid you for writers. It cannot copy a room of people who already trust each other.

## Designing the membership

Four decisions, made deliberately.

| Decision | What to decide | What goes wrong without it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is behind the wall | Things that depend on trust: data, source documents, the editor's working notes, members' questions to each other | The wall becomes a paywall on content readers can get elsewhere |
| Rituals | A fixed time when members expect each other: a weekly call with an agenda, a Monday thread, an annual gathering | No peer value; members meet the content, not each other |
| Recognition | Contributors named in the work; access to the editor that readers do not get | The people doing the sourcing stop doing it |
| A members' council | Six to ten members, rotating, meeting quarterly | Drift goes unnoticed and recruitment has no advocates |

Keep the public layer strong enough to recruit from. Rituals are the mechanism for peer value: without them, the wall is just a paywall. An annual gathering can be twenty people in a borrowed room. Recognition costs attention, not money, and it is the cheapest retention tool you have. The council tells you what the membership wants and when you have drifted, and its members become your first recruiters, because the role gives them something to say about you.

## The first hundred for media

[The first hundred](https://lowob.com/research/the-first-hundred/) argued that the first hundred people set the shape of everything after. For media, the test is simple. The first hundred members are the hundred readers whose job titles you would put in the sponsor deck.

That means recruiting by name, not by funnel. List the hundred. Write to each one. Tell them what the membership is for and why they specifically are on the list. Expect to do this yourself, because nobody else can. The composition of the first hundred becomes your pitch to sponsors later. It also becomes the peer value for the next hundred. Get the roles right before you get the number up.

## Owned channels only

Members live on channels you control: email, and a members' space on a platform where you hold the export and the relationship. For membership the rule is stricter than for audience: if the platform can change the terms, it cannot hold the membership.

The Reuters Institute data shows why. Social and video networks, at 54%, are now the most used route to online news, ahead of news sites and apps at 51%, and owned-site reach has fallen since 2021. A social platform group is fine for recruiting. It is not where the membership lives. The moment you depend on a feed to reach your own members, you have handed the job to someone who does not have it.

## What to measure

Four numbers, reported monthly, replacing the audience numbers you report now.

| Measure | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| Member retention | Whether the wall and the rituals are worth paying for |
| Contribution rate | Share of members who sourced, posted or asked in the period |
| Member referrals | New members who were introduced by an existing one |
| Paid revenue from referring members | Whether peer value is funding the business |

The last one matters most. If a growing share of paid revenue comes from members who brought someone, the membership is working. If it stays flat while the list grows, you have a newsletter with a paywall. [Stop reporting reach](https://lowob.com/research/stop-reporting-reach/) covers why reach reporting hides this, and our explainer on [customer churn](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-churn/) sets out how to calculate the retention figure consistently.

## lowob takeaways

- **Recruit from the list.** Subscribers, followers, opens and downloads are the pool a community is recruited from, not the community.
- **Ask for the three contributions.** Sourcing, peer amplification and peer value, explicitly.
- **Run rituals.** A weekly call or a Monday members' thread is the mechanism for peer value.
- **Report like a business line.** Retention, contribution rate, referrals and revenue from referring members, monthly.

## Common questions

### How do you turn a newsletter audience into a paid community?

Decide what goes behind the wall, set fixed rituals where members meet each other, recognise contributors, and run a rotating members' council. Recruit the first hundred personally, by name and job title.

### What is the difference between a subscription and a membership?

A subscription sells access to content. A membership is a relationship in which people pay, show up, contribute and refer, and get value from each other as well as from you.

### What metrics should a media membership track?

Member retention, contribution rate, member referrals and paid revenue from referring members, reported monthly. If revenue from referring members stays flat while the list grows, you have a newsletter with a paywall.

### Should a media membership live in a social media group?

No. A social platform group is fine for recruiting, but members should live on email and a space where you hold the export and the relationship.
